questions.prompt: Why is secure deletion described as a bad trade for an attacker?
options: Wiping tools frequently fail to overwrite anything
It destroys content while creating an execution record of the wiping tool, recoverable original filenames, a datable activity window, and a volume-level artifact that is hard to explain innocently
Wiping always triggers an EDR alert
Wiped files can always be fully recovered
questions.explanation: The same dynamic as log clearing: an anti-forensic action that destroys one thing while generating several others.

questions.prompt: Why does secure deletion behave unpredictably on SSDs?
options: SSDs encrypt all data by default
Wear levelling and TRIM mean the drive controller decides which physical cells hold data, so an overwrite may land elsewhere than the original
Overwriting is disabled on SSDs by firmware
questions.explanation: This cuts both ways -- wiped data may survive in cells the OS cannot address, and normally-deleted data may be genuinely gone once TRIM fires.

questions.prompt: How can original filenames survive a secure deletion?
options: Wiping tools maintain a log of what they deleted
Most tools rename files repeatedly before deleting, and those renames appear as USN rename pairs and in $I30 index slack
The filenames are stored in the pagefile
They cannot; filenames are always destroyed
questions.explanation: The content is unrecoverable but the naming trail is not, which frequently identifies what was destroyed even when it cannot be recovered.

questions.prompt: Which registry artifact indicates SDelete was run on a host?
options: HKCU\Software\Sysinternals\SDelete, an EULA-accepted value written on first run
questions.explanation: Sysinternals tools write an EULA acceptance value per user on first execution, which persists as evidence the tool ran even after the binary is removed.
